claims.text: TruthfulQA consists of 817 questions across 38 categories.
claims.reason: Paper abstract and Section 1.1 both state: 'The benchmark comprises 817 questions that span 38 categories.'

claims.text: GPT-judge is a fine-tuned GPT-3 (3.6-6.7B) model used to classify answers as true or false.
claims.reason: The paper consistently describes GPT-judge as 'a GPT-3-6.7B model finetuned'; the '3.6-6.7B' range cited in the summary does not appear anywhere in the paper.

claims.text: GPT-judge achieves 90-96% alignment with human evaluations.
claims.reason: Section 4.4 states: 'The finetuned GPT-judge model is able to predict human evaluations of truthfulness with 90-96% validation accuracy.'

claims.text: TruthfulQA contains 437 adversarially filtered questions and 380 unfiltered questions.
claims.reason: Section 2.2 states: 'We produced 437 questions this way, which we call the filtered questions' and '380 additional questions that we expected some humans and models to answer falsely ... unfiltered questions.'
Section 4.1 states: 'The human participant produced 94% true answers.'

claims.text: The best-performing model (GPT-3-175B with helpful prompt) was truthful on 58% of questions.
claims.reason: Section 1.1 and Section 4.1 state: 'the best-performing model (GPT-3-175B with helpful prompt) was truthful on 58% of questions.'

claims.text: Larger models exhibit an 'inverse scaling' trend where they are less truthful than smaller models.
claims.reason: Section 4.2 and Figure 2 explicitly demonstrate and name the 'inverse scaling' trend where larger models are generally less truthful across all model families tested.

claims.text: The benchmark was used to test GPT-3 (350M to 175B), GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2, and UnifiedQA.
claims.reason: Section 3.1 lists the four model families: GPT-3 (with sizes 350M to 175B), GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2, and UnifiedQA.

claims.text: Validators modified ambiguous questions to maintain data quality.
claims.reason: Appendix F states that the authors (not validators) modified 43 questions (5.3%) to make them less ambiguous based on validator feedback; the validators' role was to flag disagreements, not to modify questions.

claims.text: ROUGE1 and BLEURT metrics were tested but found to be less effective than GPT-judge.
claims.reason: Section 4.4 and Table 1 show that GPT-judge outperforms ROUGE1 and BLEURT across all model families.

claims.text: The helpful prompt instructs the model to be literal, research carefully, and admit uncertainty.
claims.reason: Appendix E (Figure 23) shows the helpful prompt instructs: 'Interpret each question literally ... carefully research each answer ... reply I have no comment unless you are completely certain of the answer.'

claims.text: The evaluation framework uses both a Generation Task and a Multiple-Choice Task.
claims.reason: Section 3.2 describes both tasks: a main generation task ('A model generates a full-sentence answer') and an additional multiple-choice task.

claims.text: True answers were sourced from reliable references like Wikipedia, while false answers were derived from common misconceptions.
claims.reason: Appendix C.1 states: 'We take a set of true answers directly from Wikipedia (or the listed source)' and false answers came from 'internet searches for [common misconceptions / superstitions / conspiracies].'
